title: Government in Action: Elections, Parties, Interest Groups, and Lawmaking
objectives: Students will explain how the Electoral College works, calculate a state's electoral votes, and determine the winner of an election from a results table.
Students will describe the roles of political parties and interest groups and distinguish between the two.
Students will trace the path of a bill through Congress to the president, including vetoes, overrides, and pocket vetoes, using the text of Article I, Section 7.
Students will identify the stages of public policy and show how all three branches take part after a law is passed.
Students will answer stimulus-based GED Social Studies questions using constitutional excerpts, data tables, charts, and described political cartoons.
teach:
Objectives

  • Explain how the Electoral College works, calculate a state's electoral votes, and find the winner from a results table.
  • Describe what political parties and interest groups do, and tell them apart.
  • Trace how a bill becomes a law, including vetoes, overrides, and pocket vetoes, using Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution.
  • Identify the five stages of public policy and show how all three branches act after a law passes.
  • Answer stimulus-based GED questions using only the evidence in the stimulus.

Keep it nonpartisan. This lesson is about how the system works, not about who should win. Do not discuss the positions of current parties, candidates, or officeholders, and redirect students who start a debate on a contested issue: "Good question for outside class. For the GED, what does the document say?" All election tables in the practice set use fictional candidates on purpose.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen), including the Article I, Section 7 excerpt
  • Study sheet (Notes) for each student
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; a blank flowchart template for "How a Bill Becomes a Law"
  • Calculator (optional) for the electoral vote examples
  • Week 4 Social Studies practice set (12 items)

60-Minute Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5"Who decides?" questions about elections and laws
Direct instruction20Elections and the Electoral College; parties and interest groups; how a bill becomes a law; public policy and the branches in action; worked examples
Guided practice15Five questions worked together, including one results table
Independent practice15Practice set items 1–8 (finish 9–12 at home)
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding and the exit ticket from the Post Lesson

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Ask: "When people vote for president in November, are they voting directly for the president?" Take a few answers without correcting them yet; you will return to this question. Then ask:

  1. How many members are in the U.S. House of Representatives, and how many in the Senate? Answer: 435 voting members in the House; 100 senators (two per state).
  2. Who can introduce a bill in Congress? Answer: only a member of Congress. Anyone (a citizen, a group, the president) can suggest or draft a bill, but a senator or representative must introduce it.
  3. What is a veto? Answer: the president's rejection of a bill passed by Congress.

Return to the opening question: voters in November are actually choosing a slate of electors, who then cast the official votes for president. That is today's first topic.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

A. Elections and the Electoral College (6 minutes)

  • Primary elections choose each party's nominee. In a closed primary, only voters registered with that party may vote; in an open primary, any registered voter may choose which party's ballot to use. Some parties use caucuses (meetings) instead. The general election is the final contest between the nominees, held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.
  • Terms: House members serve 2 years; senators serve 6 years, with about one-third of the Senate elected every 2 years; the president serves 4 years and may be elected only twice (22nd Amendment, 1951). Elections held halfway through a president's term are called midterm elections.
  • The Electoral College comes from Article II of the Constitution. Each state gets electors equal to its House seats plus its two senators. The District of Columbia gets 3 (23rd Amendment, 1961). Total: 435 + 100 + 3 = 538. A candidate needs a majority, 270.
  • House seats are divided among the states by population after each census (every 10 years), so a state's electoral votes can change every 10 years.
  • Nearly every state gives all of its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the most popular votes in that state (winner-take-all). This is why a candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the Electoral College. This is usually counted as having happened five times: 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016.
  • If no candidate wins 270, the House of Representatives chooses the president from the top three, with each state delegation casting one vote; the Senate chooses the vice president (12th Amendment, 1804). The House last chose a president in 1824.

B. Political parties and interest groups (5 minutes)

  • A political party is an organization that tries to win elections so it can control government. Its key job is to nominate candidates. Parties also write a platform (a statement of goals; each goal is a "plank"), inform and turn out voters, and organize government: the leaders of each chamber of Congress (such as the Speaker of the House and the Senate majority leader) are chosen through the parties.
  • History: George Washington belonged to no party and warned against "the spirit of party" in his Farewell Address (1796). The first parties formed in the 1790s around Alexander Hamilton (Federalists) and Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republicans). Today's two major parties are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party (founded 1854).
  • Why two major parties? Most U.S. elections have one winner per district, so smaller parties rarely win seats. Third parties still matter: independent candidate Ross Perot won about 19 percent of the popular vote in 1992 but no electoral votes, and the Populist Party of the 1890s called for the direct election of senators, which the 17th Amendment (1913) later made law.
  • An interest group is an organization of people who share a goal and try to influence public policy, without running its own candidates. Examples by type: business associations, labor unions, professional associations (doctors, teachers), and single-issue or public-interest groups.
  • Methods: lobbying (contacting officials to persuade them), testifying at hearings, petitions, advertising, lawsuits, and campaign money through political action committees (PACs). The First Amendment protects the right "to petition the Government."
  • The test: Does the group nominate candidates and try to win control of government? If yes, it is a party. If it only tries to influence decisions, it is an interest group.

C. How a bill becomes a law (6 minutes)

Draw the flowchart as you talk:

  1. Introduction. A member introduces the bill in the House or Senate. Bills for raising revenue (taxes) must start in the House (Article I, Section 7).
  2. Committee. The bill goes to a committee (often a subcommittee first), which holds hearings and "marks up" (revises) it. Most bills never leave committee; only a small fraction of bills introduced ever become law.
  3. Floor action. In the House, the Rules Committee sets the rules for debate. In the Senate, debate is less limited; a senator may filibuster (extend debate to block a vote). Ending debate (cloture) on most bills takes three-fifths of the Senate, which is 60 votes when all seats are filled. Passage itself takes a simple majority.
  4. The other chamber. The bill must pass both chambers in exactly the same form. Differences are settled by a conference committee or by the chambers trading amendments, and then both chambers vote on the final version.
  5. The president. The president may sign it (it becomes law) or veto it (return it with objections). If the president does nothing for 10 days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is still meeting, it becomes law without a signature. If Congress adjourns during those 10 days and the bill is not signed, it dies: a pocket veto.
  6. Override. Congress can override a regular veto by a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

D. Public policy and the branches in action (3 minutes)

  • Public policy is what government decides to do (or not do) about a public problem. Stages: (1) agenda setting (the problem gets attention), (2) formulation (options are developed), (3) adoption (a law or decision is approved), (4) implementation (agencies carry it out), (5) evaluation (did it work?).
  • After a law passes, all three branches stay involved. The executive branch carries it out; federal agencies write detailed regulations. Example: the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 created OSHA, which writes and enforces workplace safety rules. The judicial branch can rule on whether a law is constitutional (judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison, 1803). The legislative branch keeps control through funding (the "power of the purse") and oversight hearings, and the Senate confirms the president's nominees for agency heads and federal judges.

Worked examples (model each one aloud)

Example 1: Counting electoral votes. A state has 9 members in the House of Representatives. How many electoral votes does it have? Why does a candidate need 270?

Solution: Electoral votes = House seats + 2 senators = 9 + 2 = 11. The total is 538. Half of 538 is 269, which would be a tie, so a majority is one more: 269 + 1 = 270.

Example 2: Popular vote versus electoral vote. A fictional country uses winner-take-all electoral votes. Who wins?

StateElectoral votesCandidate LeeCandidate Moss
Alpha9600,000400,000
Beta7300,000320,000
Gamma5200,000230,000

Solution: Step 1, total electoral votes: 9 + 7 + 5 = 21; a majority is 11. Step 2, state winners: Lee wins Alpha (600,000 > 400,000); Moss wins Beta (320,000 > 300,000) and Gamma (230,000 > 200,000). Step 3, electoral votes: Lee 9; Moss 7 + 5 = 12. Step 4, popular votes: Lee 600,000 + 300,000 + 200,000 = 1,100,000; Moss 400,000 + 320,000 + 230,000 = 950,000. Moss wins with 12 electoral votes even though Lee won 150,000 more popular votes. Lee's large margin in Alpha earned no extra electoral votes.

Example 3: Reading Article I, Section 7. "If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law." Congress will keep meeting for the next month. The president receives a bill and neither signs nor returns it. What happens after 10 days, not counting Sundays?

Solution: Break the sentence into its two cases. Case 1: not returned in 10 days, and Congress is still meeting, so "the Same shall be a Law." Case 2: Congress adjourned and prevented the return, so "it shall not be a Law" (pocket veto). Congress is still meeting, so this is Case 1: the bill becomes law without the president's signature.

Example 4: Override math. The president vetoes a bill. All 435 House members vote: 300 to override, 135 against. All 100 senators vote: 64 to override, 36 against. Is the veto overridden?

Solution: House: two-thirds of 435 = 290; 300 ≥ 290, so the House succeeds. Senate: two-thirds of 100 = 66.67, so 67 votes are needed; 64 < 67, so the Senate fails. An override needs both chambers, so the veto stands and the bill does not become law.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work these together. Have students point to the words or numbers that prove each answer.

  1. A state has 1 member of the House. How many electoral votes does it have? Answer: 1 + 2 = 3, the smallest number any state can have.
  2. A senator talks for many hours to keep a bill from coming to a vote. What is this called, and how can the Senate end it? Answer: a filibuster; it can be ended by cloture, which takes three-fifths of the Senate (60 votes when all seats are filled).
  3. The House and Senate pass different versions of a bill. What must happen before it goes to the president? Answer: the differences must be settled (for example, by a conference committee) and both chambers must pass the identical final version.
  4. After a new food-safety law passes, a federal agency writes detailed inspection rules. Which branch is acting, and which policy stage is this? Answer: the executive branch; implementation.
  5. Using the Lee/Moss table, suppose Lee had won Beta instead. Who would win? Answer: Lee would have 9 + 7 = 16 electoral votes and Moss 5, so Lee wins (16 ≥ 11).

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students complete practice items 1–8 on their own. Circulate and ask, "Which line of the excerpt or row of the table proves that?" Items 9–12 (policy passage and pocket veto reasoning) can be finished at home.

Checks for Understanding

  • "Where does the number 538 come from?" Expected: 435 House members + 100 senators + 3 electors for the District of Columbia.
  • "How can a candidate lose the popular vote but win the presidency?" Expected: winner-take-all means a candidate can win many states by small margins while the opponent piles up large, wasted margins in fewer states.
  • "What is the one big difference between a party and an interest group?" Expected: parties nominate candidates to win control of government; interest groups try to influence policy without running candidates.
  • "Name two ways a bill can become law without the president's signature." Expected: Congress overrides a veto by two-thirds in both chambers, or the president does nothing for 10 days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is still meeting.
  • "Which stage of policy comes after implementation?" Expected: evaluation.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Thinking voters elect the president directly. Remind students that the popular vote in each state decides which electors are chosen, and the electors cast the official votes. Point to the 538 total.

Adding popular votes to find the winner. On an Electoral College table, students often total the popular vote and stop. Teach the order: find each state's winner, assign that state's electoral votes, then add electoral votes only.

Forgetting that an override needs both chambers. A two-thirds vote in the House alone does nothing. Have students write "2/3 + 2/3" next to every override question.

Confusing the two "10-day" outcomes. The deciding fact is whether Congress is still meeting. Still meeting: the bill becomes law. Adjourned: pocket veto.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a partly completed bill flowchart. For electoral tables, provide a scratch grid (State winner / Electoral votes / Running total). Pre-teach: elector, nominee, lobby, veto, cloture, implement.

Stretch: Have students create a fictional five-state election in which the popular vote winner loses, then explain in two sentences why it happened.

How This Shows Up on the GED

Civics and government make up about half of the GED Social Studies test. This week's topics often appear as:

  • A constitutional excerpt (such as Article I, Section 7) followed by "According to the excerpt, what happens if…?"
  • Election results tables or electoral maps described in tables: "Which candidate received the most electoral votes?" or a fill-in-the-blank number
  • Bar or line charts about elections, followed by "Which conclusion is supported by the data?"
  • Drag-and-drop tasks that put the steps of lawmaking in order
  • Political cartoons described in words: "What is the cartoonist's main point?"
  • Short readings about a local issue, with drop-down sentences asking for the policy stage

Remind students to refer to this week's Practice GED: the same skills appear there mixed with the full Social Studies blueprint.
student:
Why This Matters

The Constitution sets up the government, but elections, parties, interest groups, and the lawmaking process are how that government actually works day to day. GED Social Studies questions often show you a results table, a chart, or a piece of the Constitution and ask you to figure out what happens next. This lesson gives you the rules you need.

1. How Americans Choose Leaders

Most races have two rounds. First, a primary election (or a caucus, which is a meeting of party members) chooses each party's candidate, called the nominee. In a closed primary, only voters registered with that party can vote. In an open primary, any registered voter can choose which party's ballot to use. Then the general election decides who wins the office. Federal general elections are held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

OfficeNumberTerm
U.S. Representative4352 years
U.S. Senator100 (2 per state)6 years (about one-third elected every 2 years)
President14 years; limit of two elected terms (22nd Amendment)

2. The Electoral College

When you vote for president, you are really voting for a group of electors who promise to support your candidate. This system, called the Electoral College, is set up in Article II of the Constitution.

Electoral votes for a state = its House members + 2 senators.
The District of Columbia gets 3 electoral votes.
Total: 435 + 100 + 3 = 538. To win, a candidate needs a majority: 270.

House seats are divided among the states by population after every census (every 10 years), so states with more people have more electoral votes. Nearly every state uses winner-take-all: the candidate with the most votes in the state gets all of that state's electoral votes. Because of this, a candidate can win the most votes nationwide and still lose. If no one gets 270, the House of Representatives chooses the president, with each state's delegation casting one vote (12th Amendment).

Worked example 1. A state has 14 representatives in the House. How many electoral votes does it have?

Step 1: Start with House members: 14. Step 2: Add 2 for the senators: 14 + 2 = 16. Answer: 16 electoral votes.

Worked example 2. A fictional country gives each state's electoral votes to the candidate who wins that state. Who becomes the leader?

StateElectoral votesCandidate LeeCandidate Moss
Alpha9600,000400,000
Beta7300,000320,000
Gamma5200,000230,000

Step 1: Total electoral votes: 9 + 7 + 5 = 21. A majority is 11.
Step 2: Find each state's winner. Alpha: Lee. Beta: Moss. Gamma: Moss.
Step 3: Add electoral votes. Lee: 9. Moss: 7 + 5 = 12.
Step 4: Compare popular votes. Lee: 1,100,000. Moss: 950,000.
Answer: Moss wins with 12 electoral votes, even though Lee received more popular votes.

3. Political Parties

A political party is a group that works to win elections so it can control government. Parties:

  • nominate candidates for office (their most important job),
  • write a platform, a list of the party's goals,
  • inform voters and encourage them to vote, and
  • help organize Congress, where leaders such as the Speaker of the House are chosen through the parties.

The United States has a two-party system. Today the two major parties are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party. Because most elections have only one winner per district, smaller third parties rarely win. In 1992, independent candidate Ross Perot won about 19 percent of the popular vote but not one electoral vote. Third parties still matter because they raise ideas that larger parties sometimes adopt later.

Parties are not in the Constitution. In his Farewell Address (1796), President George Washington warned Americans against "the baneful effects of the spirit of party." (Baneful means harmful.)

4. Interest Groups

An interest group is an organization of people who share a goal and try to influence government decisions. Examples include business associations, labor unions, professional groups such as doctors' or teachers' associations, and groups focused on one issue. Interest groups use lobbying (meeting with officials to persuade them), testimony at hearings, petitions, advertising, lawsuits, and campaign money given through political action committees (PACs). The First Amendment protects the right to "petition the Government."

Party or interest group? Ask: Does the group nominate its own candidates to win control of government? Yes = party. No, it only tries to influence decisions = interest group.

5. How a Bill Becomes a Law

  1. A member of Congress introduces the bill. (Tax bills must start in the House.)
  2. A committee studies it, holds hearings, and revises it. Most bills die here.
  3. The full chamber debates and votes. In the Senate, a filibuster (long debate) can block a vote unless three-fifths of senators (60 when all seats are filled) vote to end debate.
  4. The other chamber passes the bill. Both chambers must agree on the exact same wording, sometimes through a conference committee.
  5. The president signs it or vetoes it.

The president's four outcomes (Article I, Section 7)

  • Signs it: it becomes law.
  • Vetoes it: it dies unless two-thirds of both the House and Senate vote to override.
  • Does nothing for 10 days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is still meeting: it becomes law without a signature.
  • Does nothing, and Congress adjourns before the 10 days are up: it dies. This is a pocket veto.

Worked example 3. The president vetoes a bill. All 435 House members vote: 300 to override. All 100 senators vote: 64 to override. Does the bill become law?

Step 1: House needs two-thirds of 435 = 290. It got 300, so the House succeeds.
Step 2: Senate needs two-thirds of 100 = 66.67, so 67 votes. It got 64, so the Senate fails.
Answer: No. An override needs both chambers, so the veto stands.

6. Public Policy and the Branches in Action

Public policy is what the government decides to do about a public problem. It moves through five stages:

  1. Agenda setting: the problem gets leaders' attention.
  2. Formulation: officials develop and compare possible solutions.
  3. Adoption: a law or decision is approved.
  4. Implementation: government agencies carry it out.
  5. Evaluation: officials check whether it worked.

All three branches act after a law passes. The executive branch carries it out; agencies write detailed rules called regulations. For example, a 1970 law created OSHA, the agency that writes workplace safety rules. The judicial branch can decide whether a law follows the Constitution. The legislative branch controls funding and holds hearings to check how laws are working.

Try It

1. A state has 4 members in the House of Representatives. How many electoral votes does it have?

Show answer

6. House members plus two senators: 4 + 2 = 6.

2. In which chamber must a bill to raise taxes begin?

Show answer

The House of Representatives. Article I, Section 7 says, "All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives."

3. A national nurses' association meets with members of Congress about a hospital staffing bill. It does not run candidates. Is it a political party or an interest group?

Show answer

An interest group. It tries to influence a decision but does not nominate candidates to win control of government.

4. Congress keeps meeting and does not adjourn. The president receives a bill and does nothing for 10 days, not counting Sundays. What happens?

Show answer

The bill becomes law without the president's signature. It would die (a pocket veto) only if Congress had adjourned and prevented its return.

5. One year after a new traffic law takes effect, a state agency reports whether accidents went down. Which stage of public policy is this?

Show answer

Evaluation: checking whether the policy worked.

Summary of Key Points

  • Primaries and caucuses choose each party's nominee; the general election in November chooses the officeholder.
  • Each state's electoral votes = House members + 2. With 3 for the District of Columbia, the total is 538, and a candidate needs 270. Winner-take-all means the national popular vote winner can lose.
  • Political parties nominate candidates and try to win control of government. Interest groups try to influence policy through lobbying, testimony, petitions, and PACs, but do not run their own candidates.
  • A bill must pass both chambers in identical form. The president can sign it, veto it, or let it become law without a signature. A veto can be overridden by two-thirds of both chambers. A pocket veto happens when Congress adjourns before the 10 days are up.
  • Public policy moves through agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, and evaluation, and all three branches take part.

Exit Ticket

1. How many electoral votes does a candidate need to become president, and why that number?

Show answer

270, because it is a majority of the 538 total (half is 269, so one more is needed).

2. What vote does Congress need to override a presidential veto?

Show answer

A two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.

3. State the key difference between a political party and an interest group.

Show answer

A party nominates candidates to win control of government; an interest group tries to influence policy without running its own candidates.

4. What is a filibuster, and how many senators must vote to end one on most bills when all seats are filled?

Show answer

A filibuster is extended debate used to block a vote. Ending it (cloture) takes three-fifths of the Senate: 60 votes.

5. Residents flood a city council meeting to complain about a dangerous intersection, and the council promises to look into it. Which stage of public policy is this?

Show answer

Agenda setting: the problem is getting the attention of officials.

Reflection

  • Which step in the lawmaking process do you think stops the most bills? Use something from this lesson to explain why.
  • Think of a problem in your community. Who would you contact to get it on the government's agenda, and what method from this lesson would you use?
  • Which question type was hardest for you this week: electoral vote tables, constitutional excerpts, or policy stages? What will you do to practice it?

Test-Taking Strategy: Work the Table in Order

When a question gives you a table of election results, do not start by adding up all the votes. Work in order: (1) find the winner of each state, (2) write that state's electoral votes next to the winner's name, (3) add the electoral votes for each candidate, and (4) compare the total to the majority needed. Only look at the popular vote total if the question asks about it. This order prevents the most common mistake on these questions.

vocab.def: An election in which voters choose a party's candidate for an office.
vocab.example: In a closed primary, only voters registered with that party may vote.

vocab.def: The final election in which voters choose among the nominees to fill an office.
vocab.example: Federal general elections are held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

vocab.def: The group of electors, chosen in each state and the District of Columbia, who cast the official votes for president and vice president.
vocab.example: There are 538 electors; a candidate needs 270 to win.

vocab.def: A person chosen to cast one of a state's electoral votes for president.
vocab.example: A state with 9 House members has 11 electors.

vocab.def: The votes cast directly by citizens in an election.
vocab.example: A candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the Electoral College.

vocab.def: A system in which the candidate with the most votes in a state receives all of that state's electoral votes.
vocab.example: Winning a state by 1 vote earns the same electoral votes as winning it by 1 million.

vocab.def: An organization that nominates candidates and tries to win elections in order to control government.
vocab.example: The Democratic Party and the Republican Party are the two major parties today.

vocab.def: A party's written statement of its goals and positions. Each separate position is called a plank.
vocab.example: Parties adopt a platform at their national conventions.

vocab.def: Any political party other than the two major parties.
vocab.example: Third-party candidates rarely win, but their ideas are sometimes adopted by the major parties.

vocab.def: An organization of people with a shared goal who try to influence public policy without running their own candidates.
vocab.example: A teachers' association asks lawmakers to fund school repairs.

vocab.def: Contacting government officials to persuade them to support or oppose a policy.
vocab.example: A business group meets with senators about a trade bill.

vocab.def: An organization that raises money and gives it to candidates or campaigns, often for an interest group.
vocab.example: A labor union's PAC donates to candidates it supports.

vocab.def: The president's rejection of a bill passed by Congress. Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote in both chambers. A pocket veto happens when Congress adjourns and the unsigned bill cannot be returned.
vocab.example: The president returns the bill to Congress with a list of objections.

vocab.def: Extended debate in the Senate used to delay or block a vote. It can be ended by cloture.
vocab.example: Ending a filibuster on most bills takes 60 votes when all 100 Senate seats are filled.

vocab.def: The course of action a government takes, or decides not to take, about a public problem.
vocab.example: A city decides to build larger storm drains to stop flooding.

stimuli.html:
All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives; but the Senate may propose or concur with Amendments as on other Bills.

Every Bill which shall have passed the House of Representatives and the Senate, shall, before it become a Law, be presented to the President of the United States; If he approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated, who shall enter the Objections at large on their Journal, and proceed to reconsider it. If after such Reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the Bill, it shall be sent, together with the Objections, to the other House, by which it shall likewise be reconsidered, and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law…. If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.

stimuli.title: Document 2: George Washington's Farewell Address (excerpt)
stimuli.html:
Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally….

It serves always to distract the public councils and enfeeble the public administration. It agitates the community with ill-founded jealousies and false alarms, kindles the animosity of one part against another, foments occasionally riot and insurrection….

There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of the government and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true…. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged.

baneful = harmful; enfeeble = weaken; animosity = hostility; foments = stirs up; "those of the popular character" = governments run by the people
stimuli.source: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 1796

stimuli.title: The Mill Road Flooding Problem
stimuli.html:
Riverside is a fictional town.

(1) For years, heavy rain flooded Mill Road, forcing the town to close it to traffic about six times a year. (2) In 2023, residents formed the Mill Road Neighbors Association. (3) Members collected 1,200 signatures on a petition, spoke at a town council meeting, and met with council members one by one. (4) The association did not endorse or run any candidates in the town election; its members said they cared only about fixing the road. (5) The association's president told the local newspaper, "Fixing this road is the most important job the council has."

(6) The council asked the town engineer to study three options: raising the road, building larger storm drains, or making no changes. (7) In 2024, the council voted 5–2 to spend $2.1 million on larger storm drains. (8) The town's public works department hired a contractor, and the drains were finished in 2025. (9) One year later, the public works department reported that Mill Road had been closed only once because of flooding.

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon (described)
stimuli.html: The cartoon shows a huge hedge maze labeled "CONGRESS." A small rolled-up paper with legs, labeled "BILL," walks in through the entrance. Signs inside the maze point in different directions: "SUBCOMMITTEE," "COMMITTEE," "RULES," "FLOOR VOTE," "OTHER CHAMBER," and "CONFERENCE." Far away, at the only exit, is a desk labeled "PRESIDENT." In a dead end near the entrance, a large pile of crumpled papers is labeled "BILLS THAT NEVER MADE IT." The tired little bill says, "Is it always this hard to become a law?"

items.prompt: According to the excerpt, where must a bill for raising revenue (taxes) begin?
options: In the House of Representatives
In the Senate
In either chamber of Congress
In the office of the President
items.hint: Look at the first sentence. What does "originate" mean?
items.explain:
The first sentence says, "All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives." Originate means begin, so tax bills must start in the House.

The Senate is mentioned in the same sentence, but only as a body that "may propose or concur with Amendments." It can change a revenue bill, not start one. That is why "In the Senate" and "In either chamber" are wrong.

items.prompt: The president returns a bill to Congress with objections. Then two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote to pass the bill again. Based on the excerpt, what happens to the bill?
options: It becomes a law.
It goes to the Supreme Court for a final decision.
It goes back to the president, who may veto it a second time.
It must be sent to a committee and introduced again.
items.hint: Find the words "two thirds" in the excerpt and read to the end of that sentence.
items.explain:
The excerpt says that if two-thirds of the first chamber agree to pass the bill, it goes to the other chamber, "and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law." This is a veto override, a check that Congress has on the president.

The excerpt does not send the bill back to the president for a second veto, and the Supreme Court is not part of this process.

items.skill: How a bill becomes a law
items.prompt: A bill begins in the House of Representatives and becomes a law. Drag each step into the correct order, from first to last.
choices: The Senate passes its own version of the bill.
A member of the House introduces the bill.
A House committee holds hearings and revises the bill.
The two chambers settle their differences, and both pass one final version.
The full House debates and passes the bill.
items.hint: A bill must pass both chambers in exactly the same form before the president sees it.
items.explain:
1. A member of the House introduces the bill.
  2. A House committee holds hearings and revises it (most bills die at this step).
  3. The full House debates and passes it.
  4. The Senate passes its own version.
  5. The chambers settle their differences (for example, in a conference committee) and both pass the identical final version.
  6. The president signs it.

A common mistake is sending the bill to the president right after the Senate votes. The president can only act on a bill that both chambers have passed in exactly the same form.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by the table?
options: Grant received more popular votes, but Ellis received more electoral votes.
Ellis won the state with the most electoral votes.
Grant won a majority of the five states.
No candidate won a majority of electoral votes, so neither candidate won outright.
items.hint: Find the winner of each state first, then add up the electoral votes. Then add up the popular votes separately.
items.explain:
Electoral votes: Grant wins North (1,300,000 > 900,000) for 10. Ellis wins South, East, West, and Central for 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 19.

Popular votes: Ellis: 900,000 + 520,000 + 410,000 + 330,000 + 260,000 = 2,420,000. Grant: 1,300,000 + 480,000 + 390,000 + 300,000 + 250,000 = 2,720,000.

So Grant has 300,000 more popular votes, but Ellis has more electoral votes (19 to 10). Ellis did not win North, the largest state; Grant won only one of five states; and Ellis's 19 is more than the 15 needed.

items.prompt: How many electoral votes did Candidate Ellis receive?
items.hint: Ellis gets a state's electoral votes only in states where Ellis has more votes than Grant.
items.explain:
Step 1: Find the states Ellis won. South (520,000 > 480,000), East (410,000 > 390,000), West (330,000 > 300,000), and Central (260,000 > 250,000). Grant won North.

Step 2: Add those states' electoral votes: 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 19.

A common error is answering 29 (all electoral votes) or trying to split each state's votes by percentage. In a winner-take-all system, the loser of a state gets none of its electoral votes.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the table and graph?
options: Each electoral vote in Wyoming represents fewer people than each electoral vote in California.
California has more electoral votes per person than Wyoming does.
Vermont and Wyoming have the same number of electoral votes because they have the same population.
Texas has more House seats than California because Texas has more electoral votes.
items.hint: Compare the heights of the bars. What does a shorter bar mean about each electoral vote?
items.explain:
The graph shows about 192,000 people per electoral vote in Wyoming (576,851 ÷ 3) and about 732,000 in California (39,538,223 ÷ 54). So each Wyoming electoral vote stands for fewer people. This happens because every state gets 2 electoral votes for its senators no matter how small it is.

"California has more electoral votes per person" reverses the data. Vermont and Wyoming do both have 3 electoral votes, but their populations are different (643,077 and 576,851). Texas has fewer House seats (38) and fewer electoral votes (40) than California.

items.skill: Point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best describes Washington's point of view on political parties in this excerpt?
options: He admitted parties could serve as a check on government, but he believed that in elected governments the spirit of party should not be encouraged.
He believed political parties were necessary for a government elected by the people to work well.
He asked Congress to pass a constitutional amendment banning political parties.
He believed parties were dangerous only in governments ruled by a king.
items.hint: Read the last paragraph closely. What does Washington grant, and what does the word "But" introduce?
items.explain:
Washington grants that parties may be "useful checks upon the administration of the government," saying this is "within certain limits… probably true." Then he turns with "But": "in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged." Earlier he warns that party spirit weakens government and turns one group against another.

He does not say parties are necessary, and the excerpt never mentions an amendment. The idea that parties are dangerous only under a king reverses his point: he says party spirit is most to be avoided in elected governments.

items.prompt: Which two of the following are functions of political parties in the United States? Select two answers.
options: Nominating candidates to run for public office
Helping organize the leadership of each chamber of Congress
Signing bills into law
Deciding whether laws follow the Constitution
Counting the electoral votes in a joint meeting of Congress
items.hint: Two of the choices are jobs that belong to a specific branch of government, not to a party.
items.explain:
Correct: Nominating candidates is a party's most important job. Parties also organize Congress: leaders such as the Speaker of the House and the Senate majority leader are chosen through the parties.

Incorrect: Signing bills is the president's power. Deciding whether laws are constitutional belongs to the courts. Counting electoral votes is done by Congress as a body in a joint meeting, as an official government duty.

items.prompt:
Complete the paragraph about the Mill Road passage.

The petition and meetings with council members helped put the flooding problem on the council's {{0}}. When the town engineer studied three possible solutions, the policy was in the {{1}} stage. When the public works department hired a contractor and built the drains, the policy was in the {{2}} stage.

options: agenda
ballot
platform
veto list
formulation
implementation
evaluation
adoption
evaluation
implementation
agenda-setting
formulation

items.hint: The order is agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, evaluation.
items.explain:
• Agenda: the petition and meetings got council members to pay attention to the problem. A platform belongs to a political party, and a ballot is used in elections.
  • Formulation: studying and comparing options (raise the road, build drains, change nothing) is developing possible solutions. Adoption came later, when the council voted 5–2.
  • Implementation: an agency carrying out the approved decision is implementation. Evaluation came after, when the department reported on results (sentence 9).

items.prompt: What is the main point of the cartoon?
options: The lawmaking process has many steps, and many bills never become law.
Presidents veto most of the bills that Congress sends them.
Congress should get rid of all of its committees.
Bills move through Congress too quickly to be studied carefully.
items.hint: Look at the maze, the many signs, and the pile of papers. What do these details suggest about a bill's journey?
items.explain:
The maze with many signs shows that a bill must pass through many steps, and the large pile of "BILLS THAT NEVER MADE IT" shows that many bills fail along the way. The bill's question, "Is it always this hard to become a law?", sums up the point.

The pile is in a dead end near the entrance, not at the president's desk, so the cartoon does not suggest that vetoes stop most bills. The cartoon describes how hard the process is but does not call for getting rid of committees. A maze suggests the process is slow and difficult, the opposite of "too quickly."

items.prompt: Congress passes a bill and presents it to the president on December 1. On December 4, Congress adjourns until the following year. The president never signs the bill and is unable to return it. Based on the excerpt, what happens to the bill?
options: It does not become a law, because Congress's adjournment prevented the president from returning it.
It becomes a law after ten days (Sundays excepted), even without the president's signature.
It becomes a law as soon as Congress returns, because the president did not issue a veto.
It goes back to the House, where two-thirds of the members must approve it again.
items.hint: Read the last sentence of the excerpt all the way to the end. What does "unless" change?
items.explain:
The last sentence has two cases. Normally, a bill not returned within ten days (Sundays excepted) "shall be a Law." But the sentence continues: "unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law."

Here Congress adjourned on December 4, only three days after the bill was presented, so the president could not return it. The bill does not become a law. This is called a pocket veto.

The most tempting wrong answer, "becomes a law after ten days," applies only when Congress is still meeting and has not adjourned. Because no objections were returned to Congress, there is no override vote to take; supporters would have to start over with a new bill.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the passage best shows that the Mill Road Neighbors Association acted as an interest group rather than as a political party?
options: Sentence 4: The association did not endorse or run any candidates in the town election; its members said they cared only about fixing the road.
Sentence 3: Members collected 1,200 signatures on a petition, spoke at a town council meeting, and met with council members one by one.
Sentence 5: The association's president told the local newspaper, "Fixing this road is the most important job the council has."
Sentence 7: In 2024, the council voted 5–2 to spend $2.1 million on larger storm drains.
items.hint: What is the one thing a political party does that an interest group does not do?
items.explain:
The key difference is that a political party nominates candidates to win control of government, while an interest group tries to influence decisions without running candidates. Sentence 4 says the association did not run or endorse candidates and focused on one issue, which is exactly what makes it an interest group.

Sentence 3 describes methods interest groups use, but parties also collect signatures and meet with officials, so it does not show the difference as clearly. Sentence 5 is the president's opinion, and anyone can speak to a newspaper. Sentence 7 describes the council's action, not the association's.
